7.10.name: 7.10.md
7.10.text:
```text
if (read(read(cin, data1), data2))
```

It evaluates the return value of the nested call to the read function, which reads two sets of data into data1 and data2. If either call returns 0, i.e. no data (or no match) was read from the input stream, the if statement would fail.

This works because read returns a reference to the input stream. When cin fails, the state of cin.fail() holds true and we will not be able to write to the same input stream, which is carried over to the second read function through the returned reference. See reference manual on cin for more clarification.

7.16.name: 7.16.md
7.16.text:
There are no constrains on where and how often an access specifier may appear inside a class definition. The only rule is that "each access specifier specifies the access level of the succeeding members." (p. 269) If members are defined before the first access specifier (i.e. without an access specifier), they will be assigned a private specifier by default. Subsequent specifiers, if exist, would observe the same rule.

Members that are part of the interface are defined after the public specifier, while those that are part of the implementation are defined after the private specifier.

7.17.name: 7.17.md
7.17.text: The difference is a "stylistic" one. The only difference is the default access level. In a struct, members defined before the first access specifier are public, while in a class, they are private. We can override this default behaviour by providing a first access specifier. By convention, a struct is used when we intend to have all members of a class public, and a class is used if we intend to have private members. (p.269)

7.18.name: 7.18.md
7.18.text: Encapsulation is the separation of interface and implementation in an abstract data type. (p.254) We can use access specifiers to enforce encapsulations, which enables us to hide the implementation part of the code from the user of the class. It is useful because it simplifies the utility of an object of an abstract data type (a class). The user of the class need not to worry about the complexities of the implementation in order use the class. Moreover, it allows us to protect the member's data from public access, i.e. they can be interacted with only through a defined interface.

7.19.name: 7.19.md
7.19.text: All the constructors and the member functions should be public. The constructors because they need to be accessible whenever an object is created and the function members because they are the means by which the user of the class is able to interface with the class, for example to fetch the values of the members. The members, such as pName and pAddress should be private.

7.20.name: 7.20.md
7.20.text: They are useful when we need to allow a non-member function to access the private members of a class. They provide an easy way to include non-member functions in the interface of a class. The downside is that they could violate the main principle of encapsulated, i.e. hiding the implementation, because may require direct access private members.

7.28.name: 7.28.md
7.28.text:
```cpp
myScreen.move(4, 0).set('#').display(std::cout);
```

In the sequence of calls in the above statement, new copy of myScreen object would be handed down to the next member function with each call. That is, each function would return a new copy of *this (lvalue) for the next member to operate on. The exuction of the statement would yield the expected results. However, the scope of the new copes of myScreen is limited to the statement itself. Once, completed the objects (copies) are destroyed without modifying the original myScreen. The following statement (myScreen.display(std::cout)), then, would print the original, unmodified myScreen object.

7.30.name: 7.30.md
7.30.text: One advantage of using an explicit this is that it reminds the class creator that class members are being accessed and changed through a pointer though function, and therefore, the return value must be a reference (or at least a pointer) to the class object. This is especially important if the object of the class will be used in sequence of function calls through the member operator. See exercise 7.29. The disadvantage, of course, it adds redundant verbosity to the code--it is much more natural to say, cursor = 0 than this->cursor = 0.

7.46.name: 7.46.md
7.46.text:
```text
(a) A class must provide at least one constructor.
(b) A default constructor is a constructor with an empty parameter list.
(c) If there are no meaningful default values for a class, the class should
	not provide a default constructor.
(d) If a class does not define a default constructor, the compiler
	generates one that initializes each data member to the default value of
	its associated type.
```

(a) False. If a class does not provide a constructor the compile will generate

```text
a synthesized default constructor for it.
```

(b) True

(c) False. Every class should have a default constructor regardless of the

```text
meaningfulness of its members' default values. If the synthesized default
constructor would suffice than there would be no need in declaring one
explicitly.
```

(d) True, but also, if present, it initializes the members from their

```text
in-class initializers first.
```

7.47.name: 7.47.md
7.47.text:
It depends on how we think the users of the class would use the data. (p.295) If an implicit conversion facilitate better uses of the class without creating undesirable effect then the answer is no, it should not be explicit, otherwise yes. In the case of Sales_data, it makes little difference either way.

Benefits:

- Enforce code predictability by eliminating surprising and undesirable effects

of an implicit conversion.

- Conversions can still take place through explicit definition.

- Enforcing the use of direct form of initialization

- Syntax requirement reflects a slightly lower-level of the language that exposes its

inner mechanics. This could also be a drawback.

Drawbacks

- Adds stricter rules to initializations, which could complicate syntax.

- only single argument constructors can be explicit.

7.49.name: 7.49.md
7.49.text:
```cpp
(a) Sales_data &combine(Sales_data);
(b) Sales_data &combine(Sales_data&);
(c) Sales_data &combine(const Sales_data&) const;
```

Assuming the string constructor is NOT explicit, when we call i.combine(s):

(a) The compiler automatically creates s temporary Sales_data object from the

given string s (implicit conversion takes place through the string constructor). However, another temp copy (of the copy resulted from the implicit conversion) is created and passed as an argument to combine. After combine completes its work it returns a reference to the modified i. At this point, the copies are destroyed, because they become out of scope.

(b) Same as the above, except a reference, rather than a temp copy, of the copy

resulted from the implicit conversion is passed to the combine member function. Likewise, the temporary Sales_data object that was created by the string constructor is destroyed once combine finishes.

(c) Here, combine is const member function, which means it cannot modify data

passed to it, including i (i.e. *this). We get an error.

7.51.name: 7.51.md
7.51.text:
Because the initializing a vector with the constructor that takes size as a parameter could lead to surprising and undesired effects if implicit conversion were to be allowed. For example, consider the following different initializations:

```cpp
int x = 10;
vecotr<double> vec(x);    // create a vec with 10 elements
vecotr<double> vec = x;   // copies 10 to vector
```

making the constructor explicit, eliminates this confusion.

In the case of string, however, we could benefit from a converting constructor (i.e. implicit class-type conversion) in the case we initialized a string from a C-style string literal (const char * type). Consider the following example:

```cpp
 // implicit conversion to library string
string s1("this is a string");
string s2(s1);   // copy s1 to s1; no confusion
```

```cpp
string s1 = "this is a string";
string s2 = s1;
```

7.56.name: 7.56.md
7.56.text:
We can think of a static member as member of a given class itself (associated with the class), rather than a member of the class object (associated with the object). As such, it is created and initialized once, and shared by objects of the same class.

There are advantages to having a static member. It improves efficiency when only one shared variable would suffice for all the created objects. More important, it enables us to create and maintain a single, persistent variable through which all objects are related, for example a counter.

A static member differs from an ordinary member, in the way it is declared and defined, and the way it is accessed. Moreover, a static data member cannot have an in-class initialization, except if it is a const of integral type or a constant expression of literal type. (p. 302) Finally, unlike ordinary members, a static member can be used as a default for argument member functions and can have an incomplete type, for example it can be used in a class of the same type. (p. 303)
